The face drooping, arm or leg weakness, and sudden confusion are the most common signs of a stroke. These symptoms appear suddenly and can come and go. If someone you know has these signs right now, call 911: only emergency care can restore brain function.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Common signs include frequent urination, excessive thirst, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and blurry vision. Some people also notice slow-healing sores or repeated infections. A blood test can check for diabetes, and your care team can help you figure out if getting tested is right for you now.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Common side effects of ibuprofen include upset stomach, dizziness, and swelling of the legs or feet. Long-term use can affect the kidneys, liver, and blood pressure, and it can interfere with bleeding during surgery. If you have heart disease or high blood pressure, ask your pharmacist whether it's right for you.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
For adults 65 and older, the CDC recommends the shingles (shingles) vaccine, the pneumonia vaccine (PCV13 and PPSV23), and the flu shot every year. Your care team can tell you which ones you should have based on your health and medicines.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Pneumonia is usually diagnosed with a chest X-ray, and a doctor may also listen to the lungs with a stethoscope. If you have a high fever, coughing up blood, or shortness of breath now, please be seen today.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A heart-healthy diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, regular physical activity, and quitting smoking all help lower cholesterol. Your care team can tell you what numbers matter for you, and they can order a blood test if needed.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Floaters are tiny specks or strands in your vision that come from gel or cells inside the eye settling over time. They are usually harmless, but a sudden increase, flashes of light, or a shadow in your vision can mean a retinal tear. If that happens to you now, get your eyes checked today.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Migraines often come with one or more of: nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light or sound, and a feeling of pressure around the forehead or eyes. Tension-type headaches are usually mild, feel like a tight band around the head, and don't come with those warning signs. If a headache is sudden and severe, or feverish, or comes with weakness or vision changes, get care right away.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Most people should have a skin exam once a year, and you should bring any new moles or changes to an appointment right away. Moles that grow, itch, bleed, or change color need to be looked at. If you have many moles or a family history of skin cancer, your care team may recommend more frequent visits.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A classic heart attack involves chest pressure or squeezing that lasts more than a few minutes or goes away and comes back. It can spread to the arm, jaw, or back, and may come with sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath. Women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have atypical symptoms. If someone has these signs right now, call 911 even if they don't have typical chest pain.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Most adults should start regular screening at age 50, but that can vary based on family history or other factors. Your care team can help you figure out what timing makes sense for you.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A cold is usually milder: a runny nose, sneezing, and a mild cough. The flu is more sudden and intense: high fever, aching, and a dry cough. Flu symptoms can include vomiting and confusion, especially in older people. If you have a high fever or trouble breathing now, get care today.
